\begin{env}[7.3.8]
\label{I.7.3.8-fr}
Soient $X$, $Y$ deux préschémas ayant chacun un nombre fini de composantes
irréductibles, et soit $f:X\to Y$ un morphisme dont la restriction à
l'ensemble des points génériques des composantes irréductibles de $X$ est une
surjection sur l'ensemble des points génériques des composantes irréductibles
de $Y$. Alors on a
\[
  f^*(\mathscr{R}(Y))=\mathscr{R}(X).
  \tag{7.3.8.1}\label{I.7.3.8.1-fr}
\]
\end{env}

En effet, on est ramené (en vertu de
(\hyperref[I.7.3.3-fr]{7.3.3})) au cas où $X$ et $Y$ sont irréductibles, de
points génériques $x$, $y$, avec $f(x)=y$~; donc
\[
  (f^*(\mathscr{R}(Y)))_x
  =\mathscr{O}_y\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_y}\mathscr{O}_x
  =\mathscr{O}_x
\]
(\hyperref[0.4.3.1-fr]{0, 4.3.1}), ce qui démontre (7.3.8.1) en vertu de
(\hyperref[I.7.3.5-fr]{7.3.5}).

\begin{proof}
Suppose first that $X=\Spec(A)$ and $Y=\Spec(B)$ are affine, given by integral rings $A$ and $B$, with $f$ thus corresponding to an injective homomorphism $B\to A$ which extends to a monomorphism $L\to K$ from the field of fractions $L$ of $B$ to the field of fractions $K$ of $A$.
The homomorphism \sref{I.7.3.8.1} then corresponds to the canonical homomorphism $L\otimes_B A\to K$ \sref{I.1.6.5}.
In the general case, for each pair of nonempty affine open sets $U\subset X$ and $V\subset Y$ such that $f(U)\subset V$, we define, as above, a homomorphism $\tau_{U,V}$ and we immediately have that, if $U'\subset U$, $V'\subset V$, $f(U')\subset V'$, then $\tau_{U,V}$ extends $\tau_{U',V'}$, and hence our assertion.
If $x$ and $y$ are the generic points of $X$ and $Y$ respectively, then we have $f(x)=y$,
\[
  (f^*(\sh{R}(Y)))_x=\sh{O}_y\otimes_{\sh{O}_y}\sh{O}_x=\sh{O}_x
\]
\sref[0]{0.4.3.1} and $\tau_x$ is thus an \emph{isomorphism}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-dominant-between-integral}
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of integral schemes. The following
are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f$ is dominant,
\item $f$ maps the generic point of $X$ to the generic point of $Y$,
\item for some nonempty affine opens $U \subset X$ and $V \subset Y$
with $f(U) \subset V$ the ring map $\mathcal{O}_Y(V) \to \mathcal{O}_X(U)$
is injective,
\item for all nonempty affine opens $U \subset X$ and $V \subset Y$
with $f(U) \subset V$ the ring map $\mathcal{O}_Y(V) \to \mathcal{O}_X(U)$
is injective,
\item for some $x \in X$ with image $y = f(x) \in Y$ the local ring
map $\mathcal{O}_{Y, y} \to \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is injective, and
\item for all $x \in X$ with image $y = f(x) \in Y$ the local ring
map $\mathcal{O}_{Y, y} \to \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is injective.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The equivalence of (1) and (2) follows from
Lemma \ref{lemma-dominant-finite-number-irreducible-components}.
Let $U \subset X$ and $V \subset Y$ be nonempty affine opens with
$f(U) \subset V$. Recall that the rings $A = \mathcal{O}_X(U)$
and $B = \mathcal{O}_Y(V)$ are integral domains.
The morphism $f|_U : U \to V$ corresponds to a ring map
$\varphi : B \to A$. The generic points of $X$ and $Y$ correspond
to the prime ideals $(0) \subset A$ and $(0) \subset B$. Thus
(2) is equivalent to the condition $(0) = \varphi^{-1}((0))$,
i.e., to the condition that $\varphi$ is injective.
In this way we see that (2), (3), and (4) are equivalent.
Similarly, given $x$ and $y$ as in (5) the local rings
$\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$ are domains
and the prime ideals $(0) \subset \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$
and $(0) \subset \mathcal{O}_{Y, y}$ correspond to the
generic points of $X$ and $Y$ (via the identification of
the spectrum of the local ring at $x$
with the set of points specializing to $x$, see
Schemes, Lemma \ref{schemes-lemma-specialize-points}).
Thus we can argue in the exact same manner as above
to see that (2), (5), and (6) are equivalent.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-integral-scheme-rational-functions}
Let $X$ be a scheme with finitely many irreducible components
$X_1, \ldots, X_n$. If $\eta_i \in X_i$ is the generic point, then
$$
R(X) = \mathcal{O}_{X, \eta_1} \times \ldots \times \mathcal{O}_{X, \eta_n}
$$
If $X$ is reduced this is equal to $\prod \kappa(\eta_i)$.
If $X$ is integral then $R(X) = \mathcal{O}_{X, \eta} = \kappa(\eta)$
is a field.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $U \subset X$ be an open dense subset. Then
$U_i = (U \cap X_i) \setminus (\bigcup_{j \not = i} X_j)$
is nonempty open as it contained $\eta_i$, contained in $X_i$,
and $\bigcup U_i \subset U \subset X$ is dense.
Thus the identification in the lemma comes from the string of equalities
\begin{align*}
R(X)
& =
\colim_{U \subset X\text{ open dense}} \Mor(U, \mathbf{A}^1_\mathbf{Z}) \\
& =
\colim_{U \subset X\text{ open dense}} \mathcal{O}_X(U) \\
& =
\colim_{\eta_i \in U_i \subset X\text{ open}} \prod \mathcal{O}_X(U_i) \\
& =
\prod \colim_{\eta_i \in U_i \subset X\text{ open}} \mathcal{O}_X(U_i) \\
& =
\prod \mathcal{O}_{X, \eta_i}
\end{align*}
where the second equality is
Schemes, Example \ref{schemes-example-global-sections}.
The final statement follows from
Algebra, Lemma \ref{algebra-lemma-minimal-prime-reduced-ring}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
\label{definition-pullback-meromorphic-sections}
Let $f : (X, \mathcal{O}_X) \to (Y, \mathcal{O}_Y)$ be a morphism
of locally ringed spaces. We say that {\it pullbacks of meromorphic
functions are defined for $f$} if for every pair of open
$U \subset X$, $V \subset Y$ such that $f(U) \subset V$, and any
section $s \in \Gamma(V, \mathcal{S}_Y)$ the pullback
$f^\sharp(s) \in \Gamma(U, \mathcal{O}_X)$ is an element
of $\Gamma(U, \mathcal{S}_X)$.
\end{definition}

\noindent
In this case there is an induced map
$f^\sharp : f^{-1}\mathcal{K}_Y \to \mathcal{K}_X$,
in other words we obtain a commutative diagram of morphisms
of ringed spaces
$$
\xymatrix{
(X, \mathcal{K}_X) \ar[r] \ar[d]^f &
(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \ar[d]^f \\
(Y, \mathcal{K}_Y) \ar[r] &
(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y)
}
$$
We sometimes denote $f^*(s) = f^\sharp(s)$ for a
section $s \in \Gamma(Y, \mathcal{K}_Y)$.

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-pullback-meromorphic-sections-defined}
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes.
In each of the following cases pullbacks of meromorphic
functions are defined.
\begin{enumerate}
\item every weakly associated point of $X$ maps to
a generic point of an irreducible component of $Y$,
\item $X$, $Y$ are integral and $f$ is dominant,
\item $X$ is integral and the generic point of $X$ maps
to a generic point of an irreducible component of $Y$,
\item $X$ is reduced and every generic point of every irreducible
component of $X$ maps to the generic point of an irreducible component
of $Y$,
\item $X$ is locally Noetherian, and any associated point of
$X$ maps to a generic point of an irreducible component of $Y$,
\item $X$ is locally Noetherian, has no embedded points and
any generic point of an irreducible component of
$X$ maps to the generic point of an irreducible component of $Y$, and
\item $f$ is flat.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The question is local on $X$ and $Y$. Hence we reduce to the case where
$X = \Spec(A)$, $Y = \Spec(R)$ and $f$ is given by a ring map
$\varphi : R \to A$.
By the characterization of regular sections of the structure sheaf
in Lemma \ref{lemma-regular-section-structure-sheaf} we have to
show that $R \to A$ maps nonzerodivisors to nonzerodivisors.
Let $t \in R$ be a nonzerodivisor.

\medskip\noindent
If $R \to A$ is flat, then $t : R \to R$ being injective
shows that $t : A \to A$ is injective. This proves (7).

\medskip\noindent
In the other cases we note that $t$ is not contained in any of
the minimal primes of $R$ (because every element of a minimal
prime in a ring is a zerodivisor).
Hence in case (1) we see that $\varphi(t)$ is not contained
in any weakly associated prime of $A$. Thus this case follows from
Algebra, Lemma \ref{algebra-lemma-weakly-ass-zero-divisors}.
Case (5) is a special case of (1) by Lemma \ref{lemma-ass-weakly-ass}.
Case (6) follows from (5) and the definitions.
Case (4) is a special case of (1) by
Lemma \ref{lemma-weakass-reduced}.
Cases (2) and (3) are special cases of (4).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-meromorphic-weakass-finite}
Let $X$ be a scheme such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] every weakly associated point of $X$ is a generic point of an
irreducible component of $X$, and
\item[(b)] any quasi-compact open has a finite number of irreducible components.
\end{enumerate}
Let $X^0$ be the set of generic points of irreducible components of $X$.
Then we have
$$
\mathcal{K}_X =
\bigoplus\nolimits_{\eta \in X^0} j_{\eta, *}\mathcal{O}_{X, \eta} =
\prod\nolimits_{\eta \in X^0} j_{\eta, *}\mathcal{O}_{X, \eta}
$$
where $j_\eta : \Spec(\mathcal{O}_{X, \eta}) \to X$ is the canonical map
of Schemes, Section \ref{schemes-section-points}. Moreover
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal{K}_X$ is a quasi-coherent sheaf of
$\mathcal{O}_X$-algebras,
\item for every quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_X$-module $\mathcal{F}$ the sheaf
$$
\mathcal{K}_X(\mathcal{F}) =
\bigoplus\nolimits_{\eta \in X^0} j_{\eta, *}\mathcal{F}_\eta =
\prod\nolimits_{\eta \in X^0} j_{\eta, *}\mathcal{F}_\eta
$$
of meromorphic sections of $\mathcal{F}$
is quasi-coherent,
\item $\mathcal{S}_x \subset \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$
is the set of nonzerodivisors for any $x \in X$,
\item $\mathcal{K}_{X, x}$ is the total quotient ring of $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$
for any $x \in X$,
\item $\mathcal{K}_X(U)$ equals the total quotient ring of $\mathcal{O}_X(U)$
for any affine open $U \subset X$,
\item the ring of rational functions of $X$
(Morphisms, Definition \ref{morphisms-definition-rational-function})
is the ring of meromorphic
functions on $X$, in a formula: $R(X) = \Gamma(X, \mathcal{K}_X)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Observe that a locally finite direct sum of sheaves of modules
is equal to the product since you can check this on stalks for
example. Then since $\mathcal{K}_X(\mathcal{F}) =
\mathcal{F} \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_X} \mathcal{K}_X$
we see that (2) follows from the other statements.
Also, observe that part (6) follows from the initial
statement of the lemma and Morphisms, Lemma
\ref{morphisms-lemma-integral-scheme-rational-functions}
when $X^0$ is finite; the general case of (6) follows from this
by glueing (argument omitted).

\medskip\noindent
Let $j : Y = \coprod\nolimits_{\eta \in X^0} \Spec(\mathcal{O}_{X, \eta}) \to X$

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-widetilde-pullback}
Let
$(X, \mathcal{O}_X) = (\Spec(S), \mathcal{O}_{\Spec(S)})$,
$(Y, \mathcal{O}_Y) = (\Spec(R), \mathcal{O}_{\Spec(R)})$
be affine schemes.

morphism of affine schemes, corresponding to the ring map
$\psi^\sharp : R \to S$ (see Lemma \ref{lemma-category-affine-schemes}).

\item We have $\psi^* \widetilde M = \widetilde{S \otimes_R M}$
functorially in the $R$-module $M$.
\item We have $\psi_* \widetilde N = \widetilde{N_R}$ functorially
in the $S$-module $N$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

Lemma \ref{lemma-compare-constructions}
and the result of Modules, Lemma \ref{modules-lemma-restrict-quasi-coherent}.

$$
\psi_* \widetilde N(D(f)) = \widetilde N(D(\psi^\sharp(f))) =
N_{\psi^\sharp(f)} = (N_R)_f = \widetilde{N_R}(D(f))
$$
as desired.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-tensor-localization}
Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Then the $S^{-1}R$-modules $S^{-1}M$
and $S^{-1}R \otimes_R M$ are canonically isomorphic, and the
canonical isomorphism $f : S^{-1}R \otimes_R M \to S^{-1}M$
is given by
$$
f((a/s) \otimes m) = am/s, \forall a \in R, m \in M, s \in S
$$
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Obviously, the map
$f' : S^{-1}R \times M \to S^{-1}M$ given by $f'(a/s, m) = am/s$ is
bilinear, and thus by the
universal property, this map induces a unique $S^{-1}R$-module homomorphism
$f : S^{-1}R \otimes_R M \to S^{-1}M$ as in the statement of the lemma.
Actually every element in $S^{-1}M$ is of the form $m/s$, $m\in M, s\in S$ and
every element in
$S^{-1}R \otimes_R M$ is of the form $1/s \otimes m$. To see the latter fact,
write an element in
$S^{-1}R \otimes_R M$ as
$$
\sum_k \frac{a_k}{s_k} \otimes m_k =
\sum_k \frac{a_k t_k}{s} \otimes m_k =
\frac{1}{s} \otimes \sum_k {a_k t_k}m_k = \frac{1}{s} \otimes m
$$
Where $m = \sum_k {a_k t_k}m_k$. Then it is obvious that $f$ is surjective,
and if $f(\frac{1}{s} \otimes m) = m/s = 0$ then there exists $t \in S$ with
$tm = 0$ in $M$. Then we have
$$
\frac{1}{s} \otimes m = \frac{1}{st} \otimes tm = \frac{1}{st} \otimes 0 = 0
$$
Therefore $f$ is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
\label{lemma-spec-localization}
Let $R$ be a ring. Let $S \subset R$ be a multiplicative subset.
The map $R \to S^{-1}R$ induces via the functoriality of $\Spec$
a homeomorphism
$$
\Spec(S^{-1}R)
\longrightarrow
\{\mathfrak p \in \Spec(R) \mid S \cap \mathfrak p = \emptyset \}
$$
where the topology on the right hand side is that induced from the
Zariski topology on $\Spec(R)$. The inverse map is given
by $\mathfrak p \mapsto S^{-1}\mathfrak p = \mathfrak p(S^{-1}R)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Denote the right hand side of the arrow of the lemma by $D$.
Choose a prime $\mathfrak p' \subset S^{-1}R$ and let $\mathfrak p$
the inverse image of $\mathfrak p'$ in $R$. Since $\mathfrak p'$
does not contain $1$ we see that $\mathfrak p$ does not contain
any element of $S$. Hence $\mathfrak p \in D$ and we see that
the image is contained in $D$. Let $\mathfrak p \in D$.
By assumption the image $\overline{S}$ does not contain $0$.
By basic notion (\ref{item-localization-zero})
$\overline{S}^{-1}(R/\mathfrak p)$ is not the zero ring.
By basic notion (\ref{item-localize-ideal}) we see
$S^{-1}R / S^{-1}\mathfrak p = \overline{S}^{-1}(R/\mathfrak p)$
is a domain, and hence $S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ is a prime.
The equality of rings also shows that the inverse image of
$S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ in $R$ is equal to $\mathfrak p$,
because $R/\mathfrak p \to \overline{S}^{-1}(R/\mathfrak p)$
is injective by basic notion (\ref{item-localize-nonzerodivisors}).
This proves that the map $\Spec(S^{-1}R) \to \Spec(R)$
is bijective onto $D$ with inverse as given.
It is continuous by Lemma \ref{lemma-spec-functorial}.
Finally, let $D(g) \subset \Spec(S^{-1}R)$ be a standard
open. Write $g = h/s$ for some $h\in R$ and $s\in S$.
Since $g$ and $h/1$ differ by a unit we have $D(g) =
D(h/1)$ in $\Spec(S^{-1}R)$.
Hence by Lemma \ref{lemma-spec-functorial} and the bijectivity
above the image of $D(g) = D(h/1)$ is $D \cap D(h)$.
This proves the map is open as well.
\end{proof}

\label{I.7.3.8-fr}
Soient $X$, $Y$ deux préschémas ayant chacun un nombre fini de composantes

  \tag{7.3.8.1}\label{I.7.3.8.1-fr}
\]

## The two historical assertions are different

The original EGA I paragraph asserted a global isomorphism of pulled-back
rational-function sheaves when both schemes have finitely many irreducible
components and the morphism maps their component generic points surjectively.
That assertion is false. The errata in EGA II, printed pp. 221–222, replace the
paragraph: for a dominant morphism of integral schemes there is a canonical
map, and the map is an isomorphism at the generic stalk. A generic-stalk
isomorphism is not a global sheaf isomorphism.

These are separately bound source versions. The pinned French Chapter I
transcription preserves the superseded assertion. The later French errata
transcription contains the replacement. The pinned English discovery text
follows the replacement and explicitly notes the change. Its difference from
the older French paragraph is therefore not a newly discovered translation
error. The separate printed-page verification is evidence for the replacement;
it must not be attributed retrospectively to an older source-admission receipt.

Here $\mathcal R_X$ denotes the sheaf obtained from regular functions on
topologically dense open subsets, as in the preceding comparison of
EGA I 7.3.1–7.3.4. We write $\mathcal K_X$ for the Stacks meromorphic sheaf,
which instead inverts regular sections, meaning nonzerodivisors locally.
The distinction matters on nonreduced schemes. On an integral scheme both
are the constant sheaf of its function field; the dense-open identification
is [Tag 01RV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01RV), and the meromorphic
identification is [Tag 01X5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01X5).

## The corrected construction

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a dominant morphism of integral schemes. Denote their
generic points by $\eta_X,\eta_Y$ and their function fields by
$K=k(X),L=k(Y)$. There is a canonical morphism
$$
\tau:f^*\mathcal R_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal R_X
$$
of $\mathcal O_X$-algebras. In particular it is a morphism of
$\mathcal O_X$-modules, as asserted in the replacement. Its stalk at
$\eta_X$ is an isomorphism. No finite-type, Noetherian, quasi-compactness,
quasi-separatedness, or separatedness assumption is required.

To construct the map, take nonempty affine opens
$U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}B\subset Y$ such that $f(U)\subset V$.
Dominance gives $f(\eta_X)=\eta_Y$ and an injection $B\hookrightarrow A$
for every such pair, by
[Tag 0CC1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CC1).
The induced embedding $L\hookrightarrow K$ is the map on generic local
rings, so it does not depend on the choice of affine neighborhoods.

Over $V$ the rational-function sheaf is the associated $B$-module
$\widetilde L$, and over $U$ it is the associated $A$-module
$\widetilde K$. For example, every nonempty distinguished open in either
integral affine has the same fraction field, so these identifications agree
with restrictions, not just with sections on the full affine.
The affine pullback formula in
[Tag 01I9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01I9) identifies
$f^*\mathcal R_Y|_U$ with $\widetilde{A\otimes_B L}$.
Put $S=B\setminus\{0\}$, viewed in $A$ by the injection. Then
[Tag 00DK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DK) gives
$$
A\otimes_B L\simeq S^{-1}A\longrightarrow K,
\qquad a\otimes(b/s)\longmapsto a f^\sharp(b)/f^\sharp(s).
$$
The last map is the localization inclusion. Its associated-sheaf map is
the required map on $U$.

These local maps glue. Indeed, their formulas use the same field embedding
$L\hookrightarrow K$. Given two affine pairs and a point in the intersection
of their source opens, choose an affine target neighborhood of its image
inside the intersection of the two target opens. Choose an affine source
neighborhood of the point inside both source opens and the inverse image of
that smaller target neighborhood. On this refinement the two formulas agree.
Such refinements cover the source intersection, proving agreement and hence
unique gluing. This uses affine refinements of intersections; it does not
assume that intersections of affine opens themselves are affine.

At the generic point the pullback-stalk formula, including the tensor-stalk
identity of [Tag 01CB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01CB), gives
$$
(f^*\mathcal R_Y)_{\eta_X}
\simeq K\otimes_L L\longrightarrow K,
\qquad k\otimes l\longmapsto kl.
$$
This is an isomorphism. It is exactly the stalk conclusion of the replacement.

## What can be proved beyond the replacement?

The construction also proves two useful facts, stated here as derived
comparison results rather than additional words in the printed correction:

1. $\tau$ is injective as a sheaf morphism.
2. $\tau$ is an isomorphism if and only if
   $f^{-1}(\eta_Y)=\{\eta_X\}$ as a set of points.

In the second condition, $f^{-1}(\eta_Y)$ is the **entire** generic fiber.
The condition is not merely a bijection between sets of component generic
points; it excludes nongeneric points of $X$ lying over $\eta_Y$.

For injectivity, the map on each affine pair is $S^{-1}A\hookrightarrow K$.
Its stalk at a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ is
$S^{-1}A_{\mathfrak p}\hookrightarrow K$, which is injective because $A$
is a domain and every denominator being inverted is nonzero. Thus all stalk
maps are injective. The stalk criterion in
[Tag 0H7H](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0H7H) now proves the claim.
This does not infer injectivity from the generic stalk alone, and does not
assume that pullback preserves arbitrary injections.

For the isomorphism criterion put $C=S^{-1}A$. The prime correspondence for
localization, [Tag 00E3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00E3), identifies
$$
\operatorname{Spec}C
\quad\text{with}\quad
\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A:
      \mathfrak p\cap S=\varnothing\}
=U\cap f^{-1}(\eta_Y).
$$
The equality holds because avoidance of every nonzero element of $B$ says
exactly that the contraction of $\mathfrak p$ to $B$ is zero.
Every nonempty $U$ contains $\eta_X$, represented by the zero prime.

If the entire generic fiber is $\{\eta_X\}$, the domain $C$ has only one
prime ideal, namely zero. It is a field: a nonzero nonunit would belong to a
nonzero maximal ideal. Since $A\subset C\subset K=\operatorname{Frac}A$,
this field must be $K$. The map on every such $U$ is therefore an
isomorphism, and so is $\tau$.

Conversely, if $\tau$ is an isomorphism, its sections on the affine $U$
give an isomorphism $C\to K$. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}C$ consists of the
zero prime alone. The compatible affine pairs cover $X$, so no nongeneric
point of $X$ lies above $\eta_Y$.
The scheme-theoretic generic fiber has this point-set fiber as its underlying
space by [Tag 01K1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01K1). In this case
its affine pieces are all $\operatorname{Spec}K$ with the compatible canonical
identifications, so the generic fiber itself is $\operatorname{Spec}K$.
No dimension formula or finiteness of $K/L$ is involved.

### Why the original isomorphism fails

Take $f:\mathbb A^1_k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. Its source and target are
integral, and their singleton sets of generic points map bijectively.
Nevertheless
$$
f^*\mathcal R_Y=\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^1_k},
\qquad \mathcal R_X=\widetilde{k(t)}.
$$
At the closed point $(t)$, the map is
$k[t]_{(t)}\hookrightarrow k(t)$ and is not surjective: $1/t$ is missing.
At the generic point it is an isomorphism. The whole generic fiber is all
of $\mathbb A^1_k$, not just its generic point.

The older proof's appeal to constancy of quasi-coherent
$\mathcal R_X$-modules cannot repair this. The pullback is initially an
$\mathcal O_X$-module. It need not carry the compatible
$\mathcal R_X$-module structure required by that constancy result. Here
such a structure on $\mathcal O_{\mathbb A^1_k}$ would make multiplication
by $t$ invertible at $(t)$, which it is not.

A dominant birational morphism does satisfy the derived criterion. In the
local calculation $C$ contains $L$ and lies in $K$; if $L=K$ under the
generic-field map, then $C=K$. Birationality is sufficient, not necessary:
for any extension of fields $L\subset K$, the morphism
$\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}L$ has $\tau$ an isomorphism.
This includes transcendental and infinitely generated extensions.

## What remains true with finitely many components?

Let $X,Y$ have finitely many irreducible components, without assuming they
are reduced. Suppose every component generic point of $X$ maps to a component
generic point of $Y$. Then there is still a canonical map
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal R_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal R_X,
\qquad
f^*\mathcal R_Y\longrightarrow\mathcal R_X,
$$
and the second map is an isomorphism at every component generic stalk of $X$.
Surjectivity onto all target component generic points is unnecessary.
This is a derived comparison, not the statement of the integral replacement.

To prove existence, first note that a dense open in a scheme with finitely
many components contains every component generic point. For each component,
remove the other finitely many components. The resulting nonempty open lies
in that component, and a dense open must meet it; an open meeting an
irreducible component contains its generic point.

Now let $W\subset V\subset Y$ be open with $W$ dense in $V$, and let
$U\subset X$ be open with $f(U)\subset V$. Every component generic point
of $U$ is a component generic point of $X$ contained in $U$, and its image
is a component generic point of $V$. Hence $f^{-1}(W)\cap U$ contains all
component generic points of $U$ and is dense there. Pullback of a regular
section on $W$ therefore represents a rational section on $U$.
An agreement on a further dense open remains an agreement on a dense open
after pullback by the same argument. Thus the map on rational classes is
well-defined and respects restrictions and ring operations. Sheafification
gives the first displayed map, and multiplication by $\mathcal O_X$ gives
the second. No target component not met by $X$ entered the construction.
For instance, the inclusion of one summand
$\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k\amalg\operatorname{Spec}k$
misses a target generic point but still has the asserted rational pullback.

If $\xi$ is a component generic point of $X$ and $\eta=f(\xi)$, the
finite-component formula in Tag 01RV, followed by restriction away from the
other components, gives
$$
\mathcal R_{X,\xi}=\mathcal O_{X,\xi},
\qquad \mathcal R_{Y,\eta}=\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}.
$$
Consequently the relevant stalk map is
$$
\mathcal O_{X,\xi}\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}}
\mathcal O_{Y,\eta}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{X,\xi},
$$
the multiplication isomorphism. These generic local rings need not be fields
when the schemes are nonreduced. This proof establishes existence and the
generic-stalk result, not a global injection or isomorphism.

## Embedded torsion separates rational and meromorphic pullbacks

Let
$$
A=k[t,e]/(e^2,te),\qquad X=\operatorname{Spec}A.
$$
As a $k$-vector space $A=k[t]\oplus ke$, so $e\ne0$. Its sole minimal
prime is $(e)$. At that prime $t$ is inverted and $e$ is killed, giving
$A_{(e)}=k(t)$. The dense-open rational sheaf is therefore
$\mathcal R_X=\widetilde{k(t)}$.

For $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ the rational pullback map is
$\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal R_X$. It kills $e$ and is not injective.
This is also a genuine stalk kernel at $\mathfrak m=(t,e)$: an element
outside $\mathfrak m$ has nonzero constant term $c$, and multiplication by
it sends $e$ to $ce\ne0$. Thus $e$ survives in $A_{\mathfrak m}$.
The embedded associated point is visible directly from
$\operatorname{ann}(e)=(t,e)$.

In contrast, the defining map $\mathcal O_X\to\mathcal K_X$ is
injective because it inverts nonzerodivisors. Moreover this particular
morphism to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is flat, so its meromorphic pullback is
defined by [Tag 02OU](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02OU), case (7).
There is no contradiction: the two target sheaves are different.

There is an even sharper example using the same ring. Let
$g:X\to\mathbb A^1_k$ come from $k[t]\to A$.
The component generic point still maps to the generic point. Its rational
pullback is defined and is an isomorphism, since
$$
A\otimes_{k[t]}k(t)=k(t).
$$
But its meromorphic pullback is not defined in the sense of
[Tag 02OT](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02OT): the nonzerodivisor
$t$ on the target pulls back to a zero divisor, since $te=0$ with $e\ne0$.
Even an isomorphism of rational pullbacks is not a substitute for the
regular-denominator condition.

The conditional bridge is
[Tag 0EMF](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0EMF). It requires both that
every weakly associated point be a component generic point and that every
quasi-compact open have finitely many irreducible components. Under those
hypotheses the meromorphic sheaf agrees with the generic-local-ring
decomposition, is quasi-coherent, and computes dense-open rational functions.
The embedded-torsion example fails the first hypothesis. Generic-point
mapping suffices for meromorphic pullback with a reduced source, as in
Tag 02OU(4), but not for an arbitrary nonreduced source.
